title: Three things you should know about permafrost
gist: A climate newsletter primer on permafrost: it covers about 15% of Northern Hemisphere land, has shrunk about 12% since 1850, and holds roughly 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, yet most UN climate models omit or only partly capture its loss. Wildfires could add the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of CO2 by 2100, while plant growth and other effects complicate the net carbon picture.

insights.claim: Permafrost underlies about 15% of Northern Hemisphere land, and most of it formed during the last ice age, so thousands of years of frozen organic matter are locked away.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Sets the scale of a carbon reservoir that sits outside most emissions accounting.
insights.quote: Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere.
insights.locator: Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change

insights.claim: When permafrost thaws, microbes break down the formerly frozen organic matter and release carbon dioxide and methane, which accelerate warming and form a feedback loop.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A self-reinforcing feedback means warming trajectories can steepen beyond current policy assumptions.
insights.locator: But as global temperatures tick up

insights.claim: Rising global temperatures have shrunk the Arctic permafrost footprint by about 12% since 1850, and the pace of loss has picked up over the last 50 years.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Loss is accelerating, so the emissions contribution is likely rising rather than stable.
insights.locator: The steady rise in global temperatures

insights.claim: Only a minority of the models used in UN climate reports account for gradual permafrost loss, and none include abrupt thaw and collapse after heat waves and fires.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Official projections carry a known gap, a risk for any climate-policy or transition-pricing assumption built on them.
insights.quote: only a minority of the models that have been used in UN climate reports actually take into account the gradual loss of permafrost

insights.claim: Because permafrost loss is missing from most UN climate models, the planet is probably going to warm more and faster than current projections suggest.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Skews climate-risk scenarios toward the upside, supporting tighter-carbon-policy and adaptation exposure.
insights.quote: we’re probably underestimating how much and how fast the planet is going to warm
insights.locator: There are efforts to make sure future UN reports

insights.claim: Efforts are under way to make future UN climate reports reflect the growing permafrost science.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Watch for permafrost inclusion in the next assessment as a trigger for revised warming projections.
insights.locator: There are efforts to make sure future UN reports

insights.claim: Climate change is making boreal forest fires more intense, and those fires accelerate permafrost thawing.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Fire becomes a second feedback channel linking warming to stored-carbon release.
insights.locator: Wildfires can speed up permafrost loss

insights.claim: By the end of the century, fire-accelerated permafrost thaw could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A quantified unmodeled emissions source that could be material against remaining carbon budgets.
insights.quote: this effect could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide
insights.locator: By the end of the century

insights.claim: Across remote parts of Canada and Alaska, policy is generally to let wildfires burn unless they threaten human habitats, but some researchers argue for fighting them to save carbon trapped in forests and permafrost.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A possible shift in wildfire policy and funding toward carbon protection, creating demand for detection and suppression capacity.
insights.locator: Today, the policy across remote parts of Canada

insights.claim: Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are building a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska to flag where fires are likeliest to spread and where permafrost types would release the most emissions.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Such targeting tools would underpin any prioritized fire-management or carbon-protection program.
insights.locator: Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center

insights.claim: Yedoma is a particularly deep, carbon-dense form of permafrost from the late Pleistocene era, one of several permafrost types that differ in emissions risk.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Permafrost type matters for emissions risk, so aggregate estimates hide wide variation.
insights.locator: (Yes, apparently there are different types of permafrost.

insights.claim: Proposed responses to permafrost-threatening fires include more prescribed burns, a practice Indigenous groups have used for thousands of years, or investing in early detection and putting fires out before they grow.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Early detection and fire-management tech is a potential area for public funding and climate-tech activity.

insights.claim: About 1.5 trillion tons of carbon are locked away in permafrost, roughly twice the amount in the atmosphere.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: The reservoir is large enough that even partial release could materially change global carbon budgets.
insights.quote: There’s about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked away in permafrost, about twice the amount in the atmosphere.
insights.locator: The carbon cycle of permafrost is incredibly complicated

insights.claim: Warming lets plants move north into areas they could not previously inhabit, and their growth absorbs atmospheric carbon, which may partly offset carbon lost from thawing and fire.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Offsetting uptake means net emissions are uncertain and simple worst-case numbers may overstate the loss.

insights.claim: How much carbon a given area loses and recovers depends on fire severity, local climate and environment, and the permafrost type, so net outcomes are hard to forecast.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Expect wide uncertainty ranges in permafrost emissions estimates until these factors are better constrained.
insights.locator: How much carbon is lost from permafrost

insights.claim: The higher global temperatures are pushed, the more humans disturb complicated natural systems that scientists are only beginning to understand.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Argues for caution about tipping-point risk in emissions pathways.
insights.quote: The higher we push the planet’s temperature, the more we mess with complicated natural phenomena that we’re only beginning to understand.
insights.locator: The higher we push the planet’s temperature
